name: Cacao
partsUsed: seeds (beans), nibs, cocoa powder, cocoa butter, husks
description: A small understory tree of the tropical Americas whose pods, borne straight from the trunk, hold the bitter seeds that become chocolate. Its botanical name, Theobroma, means 'food of the gods,' and in Mesoamerica the beans were sacred drink, ceremonial offering and even currency. Today it is a beloved ingredient for heart-opening rituals, love workings and sweetening spells.
metaphysicalUses: In modern practice cacao is used to open and warm the heart, which makes it a natural partner for love, self-love and reconciliation spells. A cup of rich drinking cacao is often shared or sipped alone before ritual to raise gentle, joyful energy and to set intentions. Cocoa powder and nibs are added to honey or sugar jars to sweeten a person's feelings, and the beans, once used as money, are carried or placed on altars for prosperity and abundance. Cocoa butter makes a luxurious base for love and beauty anointing balms. When working with cacao, honor its deep roots in Mesoamerican tradition with respect and gratitude rather than borrowing ceremonies that are not your own.
medicalUses: Traditionally, cacao drinks were valued as nourishing, stimulating and mood-lifting, and the beans contain theobromine and small amounts of caffeine that gently wake the body. Cocoa butter has long been used as a folk emollient for dry, chapped skin and lips. These are traditional uses, not medical advice.
whereToFind: Native to the rainforests of Central and South America and grown in tropical regions worldwide, including West Africa. It needs constant warmth and humidity, so most practitioners buy it: look for minimally processed ceremonial or raw cacao, unsweetened cocoa powder, nibs and pure unrefined cocoa butter from fair trade and ethically sourced suppliers, health food stores and grocers.
uses: Sip a cup of warm drinking cacao before ritual to open the heart and set an intention
Add cocoa powder or nibs to a honey jar to sweeten someone's feelings toward you
Place a few cacao beans on the altar or in a wallet for prosperity
Melt cocoa butter with rose petals into a love and self-love anointing balm
Share chocolate as an offering to the ancestors or spirits on Samhain
Use cacao in a self-love bath tea for a sensual, nurturing soak
caution: Contains caffeine and theobromine; limit in pregnancy (keep total caffeine under about 200 mg a day) and with heart conditions, anxiety or caffeine sensitivity. Highly toxic to dogs, cats and other pets, so keep cacao, chocolate, cocoa husk mulch and offerings out of their reach. Some people are sensitive to cocoa or develop migraines from it.
bestTime: Work with cacao on Fridays and around Valentine's Day for love, or in the dark half of the year when its warmth is most welcome.
interactions: Its caffeine can interact with stimulants, some antibiotics such as ciprofloxacin, theophylline, and MAO inhibitors; large amounts may add to blood-thinning medication.
pets: Chocolate, cocoa and cocoa mulch are toxic to dogs and cats (theobromine and caffeine): vomiting, racing heart, seizures.

name: Coffee
description: A glossy-leaved evergreen shrub from the highlands of Ethiopia whose red cherries hold the seeds the whole world wakes up to. Legend says a goat herder noticed his flock dancing after eating the berries, and from there the drink traveled through Yemen's Sufi houses into every corner of the globe. In the witch's kitchen coffee is the herb of speed, focus and getting things moving.
metaphysicalUses: Coffee is used in folk magic to speed up any working and to break through stagnation. Add a pinch of grounds to a spell to make it move faster, or drink a cup charged with intention to sharpen the mind before study, divination or an important conversation. Used grounds can be dried and sprinkled to ground and break up heavy energy, or mixed with salt for banishing and to send unwanted influences away. Tasseography, the reading of coffee grounds left in the cup, is a beloved form of divination in Turkish, Greek and Middle Eastern traditions. Coffee also makes a hearty offering to ancestors who loved it in life.
medicalUses: Coffee has traditionally been taken as a stimulant to fight drowsiness and fatigue and to ease certain headaches, which is why caffeine appears in some headache remedies. It has also been used as a digestive after meals. These are traditional uses, not medical advice.
whereToFind: Native to Ethiopia and grown across the tropical 'bean belt' of Africa, Latin America and Asia. It can be kept as a houseplant in bright, indirect light, but most practitioners buy whole beans or grounds from grocers and roasters; choose fair trade and shade-grown coffee where you can, and save your used grounds for spellwork and the garden.
uses: Add a pinch of grounds to any spell jar or sachet to speed up results
Read the grounds left in a cup of thick, unfiltered coffee for divination
Mix dried used grounds with salt and sprinkle at the threshold to banish stagnant energy
Charge your morning cup with an intention for focus, courage or success
Leave a cup of coffee as an offering for an ancestor who loved it
Burn a little coffee bean incense or add beans to a road-opening candle spell
caution: Caffeine can cause anxiety, insomnia, a racing heart and stomach upset; limit in pregnancy (under about 200 mg caffeine a day), while breastfeeding, and with heart conditions, anxiety or reflux. Not for children. Coffee grounds and beans are toxic to dogs and cats. Hot liquid and burning beans can scald or smoke heavily, so burn only with ventilation.
bestTime: Morning is coffee's natural hour, and it works best for any spell that needs quick results, especially on Tuesdays (Mars) and Wednesdays (Mercury).
interactions: Caffeine interacts with stimulants, ciprofloxacin and similar antibiotics, theophylline, clozapine, lithium and MAO inhibitors.
pets: Coffee grounds, beans and caffeine are toxic to dogs and cats.

name: Fern
description: Ancient plants that reproduce by dust-fine spores rather than flowers or seeds, ferns puzzled our ancestors so much that they invented a magical 'fern seed' said to appear only on Midsummer Eve. Bracken carpets hillsides and woodland edges, while the stately male fern unfurls its fiddleheads in shaded hollows. In folk magic the fern is a plant of invisibility, protection, rain-calling and luck.
metaphysicalUses: Traditionally fern was grown by the door or brought indoors to protect the home and keep away mischievous spirits, and dried fronds were burned outdoors to drive away snakes and pests or, in folk belief, to call down rain. European lore holds that the elusive fern seed, gathered on Midsummer Eve without touching it, could make one invisible, and that the 'lucky hand' made from the unfurled root of male fern was a powerful protective and luck charm. Fern is a classic plant for fairy magic and woodland spirit work, and a frond tucked into a sachet is used for health, good fortune and to shield against hostile magic.
medicalUses: The rhizome of male fern was historically one of the main remedies used by physicians to expel tapeworm, but it is toxic and its use caused serious poisonings, including blindness, so it has been abandoned. Bracken fiddleheads were eaten in some cultures, yet bracken contains carcinogenic compounds and a thiamine-destroying enzyme. These are historical notes only; do not take either fern internally.
whereToFind: Bracken grows almost worldwide on heaths, hillsides and open woodland; male fern is native to Europe, Asia and North America in damp, shady woods and hedgebanks. Male fern makes a handsome, hardy garden plant in moist shade. Gather fronds respectfully from abundant stands, and wear gloves; avoid inhaling bracken spores in late summer.
uses: Plant fern by the front door or keep a potted fern indoors for household protection
Tuck a dried frond into a protection or luck sachet
Burn dried fronds in an outdoor fire as part of rain-calling folk magic
Seek symbolic 'fern seed' on Midsummer Eve in a working for invisibility or secrecy
Lay fronds on a woodland altar when working with fairies and nature spirits
Place a frond under a sickbed in folk tradition for health and recovery
caution: Toxic: do not ingest any part. Male fern root is poisonous and can cause blindness, convulsions and liver damage; bracken contains the carcinogen ptaquiloside and poisons livestock. Avoid bracken spores, which are also considered carcinogenic, and stand upwind of burning fronds. Keep away from children and pets. Avoid in pregnancy. Wear gloves when handling large amounts.
bestTime: Midsummer Eve (Litha, around June 21-24) is the fern's great night in folklore, and fronds are best gathered in summer when fully unfurled.
pets: Bracken and male fern are toxic to livestock and pets; keep animals from grazing or chewing fronds.

name: Hazel
partsUsed: nuts, wood (wands and forked rods), catkins, leaves
description: A many-stemmed hedgerow tree that hangs out golden lamb's-tail catkins in late winter and ripens its nuts in early autumn. In Irish myth, nine hazels dropped their nuts into the Well of Wisdom, where the salmon who ate them gained all knowledge, a gift that passed to Fionn mac Cumhaill. Hazel is Coll in the ogham alphabet, the tree of wisdom, poetry and divination.
metaphysicalUses: Hazel is one of the most traditional woods for wands, and forked hazel rods have long been the dowser's tool for finding water, buried treasure and ley lines. Eating hazelnuts before divination is said to sharpen insight, and a string of nuts hung in the home brings luck and fertility. Weave hazel twigs into a crown and wear it to make a wish, or lay twigs at windows for protection. In British folk magic a hazel twig was carried for protection from lightning, and hazelnuts were roasted at Samhain in love divination to see whether a match would burn steadily or crackle apart.
medicalUses: Hazelnuts are a traditional nourishing food rich in oils, protein and minerals. The leaves and bark were occasionally used in folk medicine as an astringent, though this is uncommon. These are traditional uses, not medical advice.
whereToFind: Native to Europe and western Asia, growing in hedgerows, coppiced woodlands and woodland edges; the American hazel (Corylus americana) is a fine local substitute in North America. Easy to grow in sun or part shade. Cut wand wood in winter while the tree is dormant, asking permission and leaving a small offering, and gather ripe nuts in September before the squirrels do.
uses: Cut a hazel wand or forked dowsing rod in winter for divination and finding
Eat a few hazelnuts before scrying or tarot to open your intuition
String hazelnuts and hang them in the home for luck and fertility
Weave a crown of hazel twigs and make a wish while wearing it
Roast pairs of hazelnuts on the Samhain fire for traditional love divination
Place a hazel twig on the windowsill for protection during storms
caution: Tree nuts are a common and potentially severe allergen (anaphylaxis has been reported); never serve hazelnuts or use hazelnut oil on anyone with a tree nut allergy, take care with peanut allergy, and label any food offerings. Whole nuts are a choking hazard for small children. Discard moldy nuts. Do not confuse with the North American witch hazel shrub (Hamamelis).
bestTime: Cut hazel wood in midwinter while dormant and gather nuts in early autumn around Mabon, with the Samhain season ideal for hazel divination.

name: Heather
partsUsed: flowering tops, stems (for brooms and bundles)
description: A low, wiry evergreen shrub that turns the moors and mountains of Scotland and northern Europe purple in late summer. Heather has thatched cottages, stuffed mattresses, flavored ale and swept hearths for centuries, and bees make a dark, thick honey from it. White heather is famously lucky, said to grow only where no blood has been shed.
metaphysicalUses: Heather is carried as a guard against violent crime and harm, and white heather in particular is a treasured luck charm, often given to brides in Scotland. Burned together with fern outdoors, it is traditionally used in rain-calling magic. Its tough stems bundled together make a fine ritual broom for sweeping a space clear before rites, and its flowers are used in workings to call in spirits, to honor the dead and for beauty and gentle love. Heather's long life on harsh moorland lends it to spells for endurance and longevity.
medicalUses: Traditionally, a mild tea of heather flowering tops was taken as a urinary antiseptic and diuretic, for rheumatism and gout, and as a gentle calmative for sleeplessness. It was also used for coughs and colds. These are traditional uses, not medical advice.
whereToFind: Native to Europe and Asia Minor on acidic heaths, moors and bogs, and naturalized in parts of North America. Grows in gardens in full sun and acidic, free-draining soil. Gather a few sprigs from abundant stands in late summer while in bloom, never uprooting plants on protected moorland; dried heather and heather honey are sold by herb suppliers and specialty grocers.
uses: Carry a sprig of white heather for luck, especially on a wedding day
Bind heather stems into a small ritual broom for sweeping sacred space
Burn heather with fern in an outdoor fire for rain-calling folk magic
Lay heather on an ancestor altar or grave to honor the dead
Add flowers to a protection sachet carried while traveling
Use heather honey in offerings and spells for sweetness that endures
caution: Generally considered mild, but avoid in pregnancy and while breastfeeding, and do not use long term or with kidney conditions, as it contains arbutin, which is converted to hydroquinone. Do not confuse with other heaths (Erica) when harvesting for tea. Keep dried bundles away from flame unless burning intentionally, as they ignite easily.
bestTime: Late summer from Lughnasadh into early autumn (August-September), when the moors are in full purple bloom.

name: Horseradish
description: A tall, rangy member of the cabbage family whose thick white root releases a nose-stinging fire the moment it is grated. Grown across Europe since the Middle Ages, it is one of the bitter herbs of the Passover seder and a fixture of Eastern European tables. In folk magic its sharp heat is put to work for protection, purification and driving away anything unwelcome.
metaphysicalUses: Horseradish is used much like garlic and cayenne to burn away negativity. Dried, ground root is sprinkled around the house, along windowsills and on the doorstep to drive out evil and break hexes, and it is added to uncrossing and protection powders. A piece of root carried in the pocket is said to lend courage and fierce energy, and its pungent bite makes it useful in spells to sever ties or speed away an unwanted presence. Keep it for work that needs heat and force rather than gentleness.
medicalUses: Traditionally, freshly grated horseradish was eaten or inhaled to clear blocked sinuses and loosen congestion from colds, and taken with honey for coughs. It was used to stimulate sluggish digestion, and poultices of the grated root were applied briefly as a warming rub for stiff, aching muscles and joints. These are traditional uses, not medical advice.
whereToFind: Native to southeastern Europe and western Asia, now naturalized along roadsides and field edges in many temperate regions. Extremely easy, even invasive, in the garden; plant in a contained bed. Dig roots in autumn after the first frost, when they are most pungent. Fresh roots are sold in grocery stores, especially around spring holidays.
uses: Sprinkle dried ground root around the outside of the home to drive away negativity
Add to uncrossing and hex-breaking powders and floor washes
Carry a small piece of dried root for courage and protection
Grate fresh root into a protective, fiery kitchen witch dish
Use in banishing jars to send away an unwanted influence quickly
caution: Very pungent; grate in a ventilated space and keep fumes away from eyes. Raw root and poultices can irritate or blister skin and mucous membranes, so use only briefly and patch test. Avoid medicinal amounts in pregnancy (large amounts may cause miscarriage), while breastfeeding, with stomach ulcers, inflammatory bowel disease, kidney problems or thyroid disorders, and for children under 4.
bestTime: Dig horseradish in autumn after the first frost, and work with it on Tuesdays or during the waning moon for banishing.
interactions: May decrease thyroid activity and reduce the effect of thyroid hormone medication such as levothyroxine.
pets: Can irritate the mouth and stomach of dogs and cats.

name: Beet
description: A humble garden root with a heart the color of garnets and a juice that stains everything it touches. Folklore says Aphrodite ate beets to enhance her beauty, and old European custom held that a man and woman who ate from the same beet would fall in love. Its deep red juice has long served witches as a natural ink and a stand-in for blood in spellwork.
metaphysicalUses: In folk magic beets are a food of love and attraction: share one with a partner to bind your affection, or serve beet dishes in love feasts and Venus workings. Beet juice is a classic natural ink for writing love spells, petitions and sigils, and it is used as an ethical substitute anywhere an old spell calls for blood. As a root vegetable of the earth, beet grounds and nourishes, and its rich color makes it a gentle ally for vitality and the life force. Offer beets at harvest altars for abundance.
medicalUses: Traditionally, beets have been eaten as a strengthening, blood-building food and their juice was taken as a tonic. The fiber and greens were valued for gently moving the bowels. These are traditional uses, not medical advice.
whereToFind: Descended from the wild sea beet of Mediterranean and Atlantic coasts. Easy to grow from seed in cool weather in loose, fertile soil; harvest roots when they are the size of a fist, from early summer into autumn. Fresh beets are sold in every grocery store and farmers' market.
uses: Write love petitions or sigils with beet juice as a natural red ink
Share a beet dish with a partner to deepen love and affection
Use beet juice in place of blood in old spells that call for it
Place beets on the harvest altar at Mabon for abundance
Add beet powder to a beauty or glamour ritual bath for rosy vitality
caution: Safe as food. Beets and their greens are high in oxalates, so those prone to kidney stones should limit them, and very large amounts may worsen kidney disease. Concentrated beet juice or powder can lower blood pressure. Harmless red urine or stool can follow eating beets. Beet juice stains skin, fabric and stone altars.
bestTime: Harvest and work with beets from late summer into autumn, around Mabon, and on Fridays for love.
interactions: Concentrated beet juice or powder may add to the effect of blood pressure medicines.

name: Oat
description: A graceful grass whose nodding seed heads ripen pale gold in cool, damp northern fields. Oats fed the people of Scotland, Ireland and Wales for centuries in porridge and bannock, and oatcakes were baked for the old fire festivals. In magic, oats bring prosperity, comfort and a steady, nourishing kind of abundance.
metaphysicalUses: Oats are used in money and prosperity spells, sprinkled into wallets and abundance jars, or baked into bread and cakes eaten with intention. Bannocks and oatcakes are traditional for Imbolc, Beltane and Lughnasadh, and a bowl of oats left out for Brigid on Imbolc Eve is a lovely household offering. Oat straw makes poppets and harvest charms, and milky oats are used in workings for calm, resilience and recovery from burnout. Their gentle Venusian nature also suits fertility and comforting home magic.
medicalUses: Traditionally, milky oat tops and oat straw were taken as a nourishing nervine tonic for nervous exhaustion, stress and low energy. Colloidal oatmeal baths and oat poultices are a classic folk remedy to soothe itchy, irritated skin, eczema, rashes and insect bites. Oats are also a sustaining, fiber-rich food. These are traditional uses, not medical advice.
whereToFind: Cultivated across the cool temperate world. Easy to sow as a cover crop in spring; harvest milky tops when the seeds release a white juice when squeezed, and straw once the plant turns gold. Rolled oats are sold everywhere, and milky oat tops and oat straw are available from herb suppliers.
uses: Sprinkle a few rolled oats in your wallet or a prosperity jar
Bake oatcakes or bannocks for Imbolc, Beltane or Lughnasadh
Leave a bowl of oats on the windowsill for Brigid on Imbolc Eve
Tie an oatmeal sachet under the bath tap for a soothing, calming ritual soak
Weave oat straw into a harvest charm or poppet
Sip oat straw tea when recovering from stress or burnout
caution: Generally very safe. Oats are often cross-contaminated with wheat, so those with celiac disease should use only certified gluten-free oats and ask their doctor first, since a few people with celiac disease also react to oat protein. Oat allergy and skin rashes from oat products occasionally occur. Large amounts of bran can cause gas and bloating, so drink plenty of fluid, and avoid oat bran if you have a narrowed or slow-moving digestive tract.
bestTime: Lughnasadh and the late summer grain harvest (August), and Imbolc (February 1-2) for oatcake offerings to Brigid.
interactions: Oats may lower blood sugar and add to the effect of insulin and diabetes medicines; oat bran can reduce absorption of some medicines (such as statins) and iron, so take them at a different time.

name: Onion
description: One of the oldest cultivated plants on earth, the onion was so revered in ancient Egypt that its rings were seen as an image of eternity and onions were placed in tombs. Kitchen witches know it as a tough, protective bulb that soaks up illness and ill will. Its papery skins, layered rings and sharp tears all find their place in folk magic.
metaphysicalUses: In folk tradition, halved onions are placed in the rooms of the sick or around the house to absorb illness and negativity, then thrown away the next day, never eaten. Braids of onions hung in the kitchen guard the home, and a small white onion stuck with black-headed pins makes a protective charm set in a window. Onion skins are burned for prosperity and protection or saved for dyeing ritual eggs, and an onion placed under the pillow is said to bring prophetic dreams. Onion is also used to swear oaths and to cleanse magical blades by rubbing a cut half along them.
medicalUses: Traditionally, onion was used for colds, coughs and congestion, often as an onion syrup made with honey or sugar. Warm onion poultices were applied to the chest for congestion and, in old folk practice, near the ear for earache, and a cut onion was rubbed on insect bites. These are traditional uses, not medical advice; see a doctor for ear pain.
whereToFind: Native to Central Asia and grown worldwide. Easy to grow from sets or seed in full sun; harvest when the tops fall over in late summer and cure in a dry, airy place. Onions are sold in every grocery store; save the dry skins in a jar for spellwork.
uses: Place a cut onion in a sickroom overnight to absorb illness, then discard it
Hang a braid of onions in the kitchen for household protection
Stick a small white onion with pins and set it in a window as a ward
Save dry onion skins to burn for protection or dye eggs at Ostara
Tuck an onion under the pillow for prophetic dreams
Rub a cut onion along a ritual blade to cleanse it
caution: Safe as food for people, though it can trigger heartburn or IBS symptoms. Onions in all forms are toxic to dogs and cats and can damage their red blood cells, so keep raw, cooked and powdered onion and onion charms away from pets. Cut onion juice stings eyes and can irritate skin. Do not put anything in the ear canal; seek medical care for earache.
bestTime: Harvest onions in late summer when the tops fall, and use them for protection and banishing spells during the waning moon.
pets: Toxic to dogs and cats in all forms (raw, cooked, powdered); causes anemia.

name: Pansy
latin: Viola tricolor (Heartsease); Viola x wittrockiana (garden pansy)
description: A cheerful little viola whose three-colored face seems to peer back at you from the border. Its name comes from the French pensee, 'thought,' and in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream the juice of 'love-in-idleness' makes the sleeper fall in love with the first creature they see. Wild heartsease is an old herb of love, remembrance and the mending of broken hearts.
metaphysicalUses: Pansy is carried or worn to attract love, and folk tradition says that planting pansies in the shape of a heart will reveal whether a love will prosper: if they flourish, so will the romance. In old rain lore, pansies are picked when the dew is on them to bring rain. Its old name heartsease speaks to its use in spells to soothe grief and heartbreak, and it is a flower of thoughtful remembrance, laid on altars for those we miss. Pressed pansies make lovely additions to love letters, book of shadows pages and gentle communication magic.
medicalUses: Traditionally, wild heartsease (Viola tricolor) was taken as a tea or applied as a wash for skin complaints such as eczema, cradle cap and itchy rashes, and used as a soothing expectorant for coughs and chest colds. These are traditional uses, not medical advice.
whereToFind: Wild heartsease is native to Europe and western Asia, growing on field edges and waste ground, and has naturalized widely. Garden pansies are sold at every garden center in spring and fall and self-seed happily in cool, moist soil. Gather flowers in the morning once the dew has dried, unless you want the dew for rain magic. Use only unsprayed plants for tea or food.
uses: Carry a pressed pansy in your purse or locket to attract love
Plant pansies in a heart shape as traditional love divination
Add flowers to a heartsease tea or bath to soothe a broken heart
Press pansies into love letters or your book of shadows
Lay pansies on an ancestor altar for remembrance
Scatter candied pansies on cakes for a sweet love feast
caution: Flowers are generally safe as an edible garnish if grown without pesticides. Avoid medicinal amounts in pregnancy, while breastfeeding and for children. Viola tricolor contains salicylates, so take care with aspirin sensitivity, and some people develop skin sensitivity.
bestTime: Spring and autumn when pansies bloom in the cool weather, with Beltane a favorite time for love workings.

name: Rush
description: Clumps of smooth, round, deep-green stems rising from wet meadows, ditches and pond edges. For centuries rush pith was soaked in fat to make rushlights, the poor household's candle, and fresh rushes were strewn on floors and carried into churches in summer rush-bearing ceremonies. In Ireland, Brigid's crosses are traditionally woven from rushes on her feast day.
metaphysicalUses: Rush is best known in folk magic as the material of the Brigid's cross, woven on Imbolc Eve and hung over the door or in the rafters to protect the house and its people from fire, hunger and harm, with last year's cross burned or buried. Rushes strewn on the floor freshen and bless a home, and a rushlight or rush-pith wick can be used in candle magic to bring light into dark times. Rush rings were once exchanged in informal handfastings and betrothals, so rush suits love and binding knots, and the plant's watery home links it to spring and well magic.
medicalUses: In traditional Chinese medicine the dried pith of Juncus effusus (deng xin cao) has been used as a mild calming herb for restlessness and poor sleep and as a gentle diuretic for urinary discomfort. These are traditional uses, not medical advice.
whereToFind: Native across much of Europe, Asia, Africa and the Americas in wet pastures, marshes, ditches and pond margins. Easy to grow in a bog garden or at a pond edge. Cut green rushes in late winter for Imbolc crosses by pulling single stems from the base, taking only a few from each clump. Dried pith is sold by some Chinese herb suppliers.
uses: Weave a Brigid's cross from rushes on Imbolc Eve and hang it over the door
Strew fresh rushes or rush sprigs on the floor to bless and freshen a home
Make a rush ring for a handfasting or simple love binding
Use rush pith as a wick in a homemade candle for illumination magic
Lay rushes on a well or spring altar as an offering
caution: Rush is for crafting and ritual (weaving, strewing, wicks), not for eating or drinking. Plant databases list soft rush as possibly toxic to mammals, so do not eat it, and wash your hands after cutting and weaving. Harvest only from clean water away from road runoff and farm chemicals, and never leave rushlights or rush wicks burning unattended; set them in a fireproof holder.
bestTime: Gather rushes in late winter and weave Brigid's crosses on Imbolc Eve (January 31), with summer the traditional time for rush-bearing and strewing.
pets: Possibly toxic to mammals. Grazing animals usually avoid it unless other food is scarce; keep pets from chewing rush crafts.

name: Shiitake Mushroom
partsUsed: fruiting body (caps and stems), dried mushroom, powder
description: A savory brown mushroom that grows on fallen hardwood logs in the forests of East Asia, its name coming from the shii tree and take, Japanese for mushroom. Cultivated for over a thousand years, it has long been treasured both as a food and as a longevity tonic. In the witch's kitchen it brings the grounding magic of the forest floor, decay and renewal.
metaphysicalUses: Like all mushrooms, shiitake carries the energy of the hidden network beneath the forest, of decay feeding new life, which makes it a fine ally for transformation, rebirth and recovering after loss. Cook shiitake into a nourishing broth charged with intentions for health and long life, or add dried mushroom to prosperity and abundance dishes, since it multiplies quietly in the dark. It suits grounding meals after ritual, shadow work, and earthy kitchen magic for strength and resilience.
medicalUses: In traditional East Asian practice, shiitake has been eaten as a tonic food to support vitality and long life and to strengthen the body against colds. It is a rich source of nutrients and savory flavor. These are traditional uses, not medical advice.
whereToFind: Native to the forests of China, Japan and Korea, growing on dead hardwoods such as oak and chinquapin. It can be grown at home on inoculated hardwood logs or sawdust blocks in a shady spot. Fresh and dried shiitake are sold in grocery stores and Asian markets; never forage wild look-alikes unless you are an expert.
uses: Simmer a shiitake broth charged with intentions for health and long life
Add dried shiitake to a prosperity feast or abundance dish
Eat a grounding shiitake meal after ritual or shadow work
Place dried caps on an autumn altar to honor decay and renewal
Grow a shiitake log as a living spell for slow, steady growth
caution: Always cook shiitake thoroughly: raw or undercooked mushrooms can cause shiitake dermatitis, a striking itchy, whip-like rash, in some people. Some people are allergic, and growers can develop lung sensitivity to the spores. Use concentrated extracts with caution in pregnancy, with autoimmune conditions or blood thinners. Never eat wild mushrooms unless identified by an expert.
bestTime: Autumn, when mushrooms rise from the forest floor, especially from Mabon to Samhain.
interactions: Concentrated extracts may interact with immunosuppressants and blood-thinning medication.

name: Wheat
description: The golden grain that built civilizations, wheat has been sown and reaped for some ten thousand years. The single ear of wheat was revealed at the Eleusinian Mysteries of Demeter and Persephone, and in the British Isles the last sheaf of the harvest was woven into a corn dolly to carry the spirit of the grain through winter. Wheat is the very heart of the Lughnasadh harvest and the turning wheel of death and rebirth.
metaphysicalUses: Wheat is one of the most traditional plants of prosperity and fertility magic. Sheaves and ears are placed on harvest altars or hung in the home to draw abundance, and wheat weavings such as corn dollies, harvest knots and Brigid's beds honor the spirit of the grain and keep good fortune in the household until the next sowing. Bake the first loaf of the harvest at Lughnasadh (Lammas, 'loaf mass') and share it in gratitude. Carry wheat grains for fertility and money, and use it in workings of rebirth, since the seed must fall into the dark earth before it rises again.
medicalUses: Traditionally, whole wheat and bran were eaten to keep the bowels regular, and wheat germ oil has been used as a rich folk emollient for dry, rough skin. These are traditional uses, not medical advice.
whereToFind: First domesticated in the Fertile Crescent and grown worldwide. Ears and dried wheat sheaves are sold by craft and floral suppliers in late summer and autumn; ask farmers for a handful at harvest, or grow a small patch from seed. Wheat berries, flour and wheat germ oil are sold in grocery and health food stores.
uses: Weave a corn dolly from the last wheat of the harvest and keep it until spring
Bake and share a Lammas loaf at Lughnasadh in gratitude
Place a sheaf of wheat on the altar or by the hearth to draw abundance
Carry a few wheat grains in a sachet for fertility and money
Sprout wheat berries in a dish for Ostara or Persephone's return
Bury wheat grains in a rebirth spell, letting go of the old to make way for the new
caution: Wheat contains gluten and is a common allergen; never use it in food or skin preparations for anyone with celiac disease, wheat allergy or gluten sensitivity, and label offerings. Dried wheat sheaves are highly flammable; keep them away from candles. Wheat germ oil goes rancid quickly.
bestTime: Lughnasadh (August 1) and the late summer grain harvest, with sowing and sprouting magic at Ostara in spring.
